title: This Prehistoric Alaskan Camp is Rewriting the History of Beringia - Nautilus
gist: A Science Advances study of the 13,800-year-old Alaskan site Shég' Xdaltth'í' in the Tanana River Valley, with over 80,000 artifacts, adds evidence of common threads between pre-Clovis and Clovis cultures and feeds the debate on the peopling of the Americas.

insights.claim: For the latter half of the 20th century the Clovis people, around 13,000 years ago, were thought to be the first to arrive in the Americas, but older sites discovered since the 1990s, some as far south as Chile, upended that theory.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Background to a long-running scientific debate.
insights.locator: When and how prehistoric humans came to the Americas

insights.claim: A new Science Advances study provides fodder for debate and intriguing common threads between pre-Clovis and Clovis cultures.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Suggests continuity between early American cultures rather than separate groups.
insights.locator: Now a new study published in Science Advances

insights.claim: The 13,800-year-old settlement Shég' Xdaltth'í' sits on a bluff over the Tanana River Valley in central Alaska, part of a vital corridor for people moving through Beringia.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Anchors the Beringia migration corridor in dated evidence.

insights.claim: Researchers radiocarbon-dated the oldest sediment layer, analyzed plant and animal remains, and examined more than 80,000 artifacts.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A large artifact sample strengthens the evidentiary base.
